passage: "Two weeks and I have hit maybe half of my plan," Harsha said, dropping the paper on the table. His mother Aparna looked at the sheet. "Why do you think that is?" "Because I made it as if I lived alone in a bubble. Look, Diwali week and the wedding trip, and none of it is on here." "So what will you change?" "Study blocks a little shorter. Football stays, that is the one thing that keeps me sane. And one evening a week with no rules, when I play what I like, no guilt." Aparna smiled. "And the plan you keep?" "The one that fits my real life." He crossed out three lines and wrote a smaller number beside each.

What was Harsha feeling about the first plan after two weeks?

subtype: Approach: reviewing and loosening an unrealistic plan [Revision]
passage: I'm Irfan, and in the first two weeks of October my perfect timetable collapsed. Four hours of study every evening, cricket at six, zero screens, every day. It looked great on paper. Then there was the bus that takes fifty minutes each way on Thursdays, Ritu's birthday dinner, and a cousin's wedding at Nani's. By the end of week two I had missed nine targets and felt guilty all the time. Ammi said, "Beta, you planned for a robot." So I sat down with the timetable and a pencil. Study blocks went from four hours to three and a half. Cricket stayed exactly where it was. And Saturday night became a proper screen evening, no guilt. In week three I missed only one target.

qa.q: How many targets had Irfan missed by the end of week two?
How did Irfan feel by the end of week two?
qa.a: Irfan felt guilty all the time, having missed nine targets on a plan that left no room for real life.

qa.q: Why did loosening the plan work better than pushing harder?
qa.a: The trimmed plan left room for travel and events so it could be followed, and keeping cricket plus a guilt-free screen evening made it sustainable.

qa.q: How might Ammi see the new timetable?
qa.a: Ammi, who said he had planned for a robot, may be relieved to see a plan made for a real person.

grounding: A student recalls a plan with no room for travel or events, then trimming study, keeping sport and allowing a guilt-free screen evening.

passage:
Tuition teacher's note, 20 November — Hemant, Class 10
For two weeks Hemant came in apologising: "I missed my targets again." His plan had six-hour study days, badminton daily and no screen time at all. It had no room for his cousin Hrithik's wedding, the two-hour drive to his grandparents' village, or Diwali week. He looked worn down and guilty. On Tuesday I asked him to bring the plan and a pencil. He made the changes himself: study days cut from six hours to five, badminton kept at the same time every day, and Sunday evening marked "screens, no guilt". He also wrote "travel days: half targets". This week he has hit every target but one. He smiled when he told me.

qa.q: How long were Hemant's study days in the original plan?
How did Hemant seem during the first two weeks?
qa.a: He seemed worn down and guilty, apologising each time for missing targets.

qa.q: What makes "travel days: half targets" a useful addition?
qa.a: It plans for real life in advance, so a trip no longer counts as failure and the plan stays believable.

qa.q: How does the tuition teacher see Hemant's revised plan?
qa.a: The teacher is encouraged, letting Hemant make the changes himself and noting that he has hit every target but one.

grounding: A tutor's note shows a student loosening an unrealistic plan by trimming study, keeping sport fixed and adding a guilt-free screen evening.
